<h5 id="backchannel-logout"><a class="anchor" href="#backchannel-logout"></a>Backchannel Logout</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>This is a non-browser-based logout that uses direct backchannel communication between Keycloak and clients.
Keycloak sends a HTTP POST request containing a logout token to all clients logged into Keycloak. These
requests are sent to a registered backchannel logout URLs at Keycloak and are supposed to trigger a logout at client side.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When the client application supports backchannel logout, that logout is usually a better alternative than the front-channel logout as communication happens directly between the client and Keycloak without a web browser
involved, which is usually more reliable. Also, when the Keycloak logout of specified user is triggered by the administrator from the <a href="#viewing-user-sessions">Admin console</a> (or other use of admin REST API)
or by the actual user from <a href="#_account-service">the Account console</a>, then Keycloak can propagate a backchannel logout request to the client applications attached to the session being
logged out. This scenario is not supported in case of Front-Channel logout because Keycloak can propagate logout to the client by front-channel just when the logout is triggered in the same browser
session, which is being logged out. That is not the case for example when session of the specific user is logged-out by the administrator from the admin console.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="con-server-oidc-uri-endpoints_server_administration_guide"><a class="anchor" href="#con-server-oidc-uri-endpoints_server_administration_guide"></a>Keycloak server OIDC URI endpoints</h4>
<div class="sidebarblock page-links">
<div class="content">
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/tree/main/docs/documentation/server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-server-oidc-uri-endpoints.adoc" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Edit this section</a>
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/new?template=bug.yml&title=Docs:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-server-oidc-uri-endpoints.adoc&description=%0A%0AFile:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-server-oidc-uri-endpoints.adoc&version=26.8.1&behaviorExpected=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20you%20want%20to%20see%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&behaviorActual=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20is%20currently%20wrong%20or%20missing%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&reproducer=%3C!--%20list%20steps%20in%20the%20application%20that%20show%20behavior%20that%20should%20be%20documented%20--%3E" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Report an issue</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="paragraph _abstract">
<p>The following is a list of OIDC endpoints that Keycloak publishes. These endpoints can be used when a non-Keycloak client adapter uses OIDC to communicate with the authentication server. They are all relative URLs. The root of the URL consists of the HTTP(S) protocol, hostname, and optionally the path:  For example</p>
</div>
<div class="listingblock">
<div class="content">
<pre class="CodeRay highlight"><code>https://localhost:8080</code></pre>
</div>
</div>
<div class="dlist">
<dl>
<dt class="hdlist1">/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/auth</dt>
<dd>
<p>Used for obtaining a temporary code in the Authorization Code Flow or obtaining tokens using the Implicit Flow, Direct Grants, or Client Grants.</p>
</dd>
<dt class="hdlist1">/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/token</dt>
<dd>
<p>Used by the Authorization Code Flow to convert a temporary code into a token.</p>
</dd>
<dt class="hdlist1">/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/logout</dt>
<dd>
<p>Used for performing logouts.</p>
</dd>
<dt class="hdlist1">/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/userinfo</dt>
<dd>
<p>Used for the User Info service described in the OIDC specification.</p>
</dd>
<dt class="hdlist1">/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/revoke</dt>
<dd>
<p>Used for OAuth 2.0 Token Revocation described in <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7009">RFC 7009</a>.</p>
</dd>
<dt class="hdlist1">/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/certs</dt>
<dd>
<p>Used for the JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) containing the public keys used to verify any JSON Web Token (jwks_uri)</p>
</dd>
<dt class="hdlist1">/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/auth/device</dt>
<dd>
<p>Used for Device Authorization Grant to obtain a device code and a user code.</p>
</dd>
<dt class="hdlist1">/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/ext/ciba/auth</dt>
<dd>
<p>This is the URL endpoint for Client Initiated Backchannel Authentication Grant to obtain an auth_req_id that identifies the authentication request made by the client.</p>
</dd>
<dt class="hdlist1">/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/openid-connect/logout/backchannel-logout</dt>
<dd>
<p>This is the URL endpoint for performing backchannel logouts described in the OIDC specification.</p>
</dd>
</dl>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>In all of these, replace {realm-name} with the name of the realm.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect2">
<h3 id="_saml"><a class="anchor" href="#_saml"></a>SAML</h3>
<div class="sidebarblock page-links">
<div class="content">
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/tree/main/docs/documentation/server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-saml.adoc" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Edit this section</a>
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/new?template=bug.yml&title=Docs:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-saml.adoc&description=%0A%0AFile:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-saml.adoc&version=26.8.1&behaviorExpected=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20you%20want%20to%20see%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&behaviorActual=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20is%20currently%20wrong%20or%20missing%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&reproducer=%3C!--%20list%20steps%20in%20the%20application%20that%20show%20behavior%20that%20should%20be%20documented%20--%3E" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Report an issue</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="paragraph _abstract">
<p><a href="https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/Post2.0/sstc-saml-tech-overview-2.0.html">SAML 2.0</a> is a similar specification to OIDC but more mature.  It is descended from SOAP and web service messaging specifications so is generally more verbose than OIDC.  SAML 2.0 is an authentication protocol that exchanges XML documents between authentication servers and applications.  XML signatures and encryption are used to verify requests and responses.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>In general, SAML implements two use cases.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The first use case is an application that requests the Keycloak server authenticates a user.  Upon successful login, the application will receive an XML document. This document contains an SAML assertion that specifies user attributes. The realm digitally signs the document which contains access information (such as user role mappings) that applications use to determine the resources users are allowed to access in the application.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The second use case is a client accessing remote services.  The client requests a SAML assertion from Keycloak to invoke on remote services on behalf of the user.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="con-saml-bindings_server_administration_guide"><a class="anchor" href="#con-saml-bindings_server_administration_guide"></a>SAML bindings</h4>
<div class="sidebarblock page-links">
<div class="content">
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/tree/main/docs/documentation/server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-saml-bindings.adoc" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Edit this section</a>
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/new?template=bug.yml&title=Docs:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-saml-bindings.adoc&description=%0A%0AFile:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-saml-bindings.adoc&version=26.8.1&behaviorExpected=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20you%20want%20to%20see%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&behaviorActual=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20is%20currently%20wrong%20or%20missing%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&reproducer=%3C!--%20list%20steps%20in%20the%20application%20that%20show%20behavior%20that%20should%20be%20documented%20--%3E" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Report an issue</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="paragraph _abstract">
<p>Keycloak supports three binding types.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="redirect-binding"><a class="anchor" href="#redirect-binding"></a>Redirect binding</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><em>Redirect</em> binding uses a series of browser redirect URIs to exchange information.</p>
</div>
<div class="olist arabic">
<ol class="arabic">
<li>
<p>A user connects to an application using a browser. The application detects the user is not authenticated.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The application generates an XML authentication request document and encodes it as a query parameter in a URI. The URI is used to redirect to the Keycloak server. Depending on your settings, the application can also digitally sign the XML document and include the signature as a query parameter in the redirect URI to Keycloak.  This signature is used to validate the client that sends the request.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The browser redirects to Keycloak.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The server extracts the XML auth request document and verifies the digital signature, if required.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The user enters their authentication credentials.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>After authentication, the server generates an XML authentication response document. The document contains a SAML assertion that holds metadata about the user, including name, address, email, and any role mappings the user has.  The document is usually digitally signed using XML signatures, and may also be encrypted.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The XML authentication response document is encoded as a query parameter in a redirect URI. The URI brings the browser back to the application.  The digital signature is also included as a query parameter.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The application receives the redirect URI and extracts the XML document.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The application verifies the realm’s signature to ensure it is receiving a valid authentication response.  The information inside the SAML assertion is used to make access decisions or display user data.</p>
</li>
</ol>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="post-binding"><a class="anchor" href="#post-binding"></a>POST binding</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><em>POST</em> binding is similar to <em>Redirect</em> binding but <em>POST</em> binding exchanges XML documents using POST requests instead of using GET requests. <em>POST</em> binding uses JavaScript to make the browser send a POST request to the Keycloak server or application when exchanging documents. HTTP responds with an HTML document which contains an HTML form containing embedded JavaScript.  When the page loads, the JavaScript automatically invokes the form.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><em>POST</em> binding is recommended due to two restrictions:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Security</strong> — With <em>Redirect</em> binding, the SAML response is part of the URL. It is less secure as it is possible to capture the response in logs.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Size</strong> — Sending the document in the HTTP payload provides more scope for large amounts of data than in a limited URL.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="ecp"><a class="anchor" href="#ecp"></a>ECP</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Enhanced Client or Proxy (ECP) is a SAML v.2.0 profile which allows the exchange of SAML attributes outside the context of a web browser. It is often used by REST or SOAP-based clients.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="keycloak-server-saml-uri-endpoints"><a class="anchor" href="#keycloak-server-saml-uri-endpoints"></a>Keycloak Server SAML URI Endpoints</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Keycloak has one endpoint for all SAML requests.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><code>http(s)://authserver.host/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/saml</code></p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>All bindings use this endpoint.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect2">
<h3 id="ref-saml-vs-oidc_server_administration_guide"><a class="anchor" href="#ref-saml-vs-oidc_server_administration_guide"></a>OpenID Connect compared to SAML</h3>
<div class="sidebarblock page-links">
<div class="content">
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/tree/main/docs/documentation/server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/ref-saml-vs-oidc.adoc" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Edit this section</a>
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/new?template=bug.yml&title=Docs:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/ref-saml-vs-oidc.adoc&description=%0A%0AFile:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/ref-saml-vs-oidc.adoc&version=26.8.1&behaviorExpected=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20you%20want%20to%20see%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&behaviorActual=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20is%20currently%20wrong%20or%20missing%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&reproducer=%3C!--%20list%20steps%20in%20the%20application%20that%20show%20behavior%20that%20should%20be%20documented%20--%3E" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Report an issue</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="paragraph _abstract">
<p>The following lists a number of factors to consider when choosing a protocol.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>For most purposes, Keycloak recommends using OIDC.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><strong>OIDC</strong></p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>OIDC is specifically designed to work with the web.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>OIDC is suited for HTML5/JavaScript applications because it is easier to implement on the client side than SAML.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>OIDC tokens are in the JSON format which makes them easier for Javascript to consume.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>OIDC has features to make security implementation easier. For example, see the <a href="https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-session-1_0.html#ChangeNotification">iframe trick</a> that the specification uses to determine a users login status.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><strong>SAML</strong></p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>SAML is designed as a layer to work on top of the web.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>SAML can be more verbose than OIDC.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Users pick SAML over OIDC because there is a perception that it is mature.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Users pick SAML over OIDC existing applications that are secured with it.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect2">
<h3 id="_docker"><a class="anchor" href="#_docker"></a>Distribution Registry v2 authentication</h3>
<div class="sidebarblock page-links">
<div class="content">
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/tree/main/docs/documentation/server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-sso-dist-reg.adoc" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Edit this section</a>
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/new?template=bug.yml&title=Docs:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-sso-dist-reg.adoc&description=%0A%0AFile:%20server_admin/topics/sso-protocols/con-sso-dist-reg.adoc&version=26.8.1&behaviorExpected=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20you%20want%20to%20see%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&behaviorActual=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20is%20currently%20wrong%20or%20missing%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&reproducer=%3C!--%20list%20steps%20in%20the%20application%20that%20show%20behavior%20that%20should%20be%20documented%20--%3E" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Report an issue</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="admonitionblock note">
<table>
<tr>
<td class="icon">
<i class="fa icon-note" title="Note"></i>
</td>
<td class="content">
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Docker authentication is disabled by default. To enable docker authentication, see the <a href="https://www.keycloak.org/server/features">Enabling and disabling features</a> guide.</p>
</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>
<div class="paragraph _abstract">
<p><a href="https://distribution.github.io/distribution/spec/auth/">Distribution Registry V2 Authentication</a> is a protocol, similar to OIDC, that authenticates users against Distribution registries.  Keycloak’s implementation of this protocol lets Docker clients use a Keycloak authentication server authenticate against a registry. This protocol uses standard token and signature mechanisms but it does deviate from a true OIDC implementation. It deviates by using a very specific JSON format for requests and responses as well as mapping repository names and permissions to the OAuth scope mechanism.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="docker-authentication-flow"><a class="anchor" href="#docker-authentication-flow"></a>Docker authentication flow</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The authentication flow is described in the <a href="https://distribution.github.io/distribution/spec/auth/token/">Docker API documentation</a>. The following is a summary from the perspective of the Keycloak authentication server:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>Perform a <code>docker login</code>.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The Docker client requests a resource from the Distribution registry.  If the resource is protected and no authentication token is in the request, the Distribution registry server responds with a 401 HTTP message with some information on the permissions that are required and the location of the authorization server.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The Docker client constructs an authentication request based on the 401 HTTP message from the Distribution registry. The client uses the locally cached credentials (from the <code>docker login</code> command) as part of the <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2617">HTTP Basic Authentication</a> request to the Keycloak authentication server.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The Keycloak authentication server attempts to authenticate the user and return a JSON body containing an OAuth-style Bearer token.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The Docker client receives a bearer token from the JSON response and uses it in the authorization header to request the protected resource.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The Distribution registry receives the new request for the protected resource with the token from the Keycloak server. The registry validates the token and grants access to the requested resource (if appropriate).</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="admonitionblock note">
<table>
<tr>
<td class="icon">
<i class="fa icon-note" title="Note"></i>
</td>
<td class="content">
Keycloak does not create a browser SSO session after successful authentication with the Docker protocol. The browser SSO session does not use the Docker protocol as it cannot refresh tokens or obtain the status of a token or session from the Keycloak server; therefore a browser SSO session is not necessary. For more details, see the <a href="#_transient-session">transient session</a> section.
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="keycloak-distribution-registry-v2-authentication-server-uri-endpoints"><a class="anchor" href="#keycloak-distribution-registry-v2-authentication-server-uri-endpoints"></a>Keycloak Distribution registry v2 Authentication Server URI Endpoints</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Keycloak has one endpoint for all Docker auth v2 requests.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><code>http(s)://authserver.host/realms/{realm-name}/protocol/docker-v2/auth</code></p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect1">
<h2 id="_admin_permissions"><a class="anchor" href="#_admin_permissions"></a>Managing access to realm resources</h2>
<div class="sectionbody">
<div class="sidebarblock page-links">
<div class="content">
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/tree/main/docs/documentation/server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions.adoc" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Edit this section</a>
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/new?template=bug.yml&title=Docs:%20server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions.adoc&description=%0A%0AFile:%20server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions.adoc&version=26.8.1&behaviorExpected=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20you%20want%20to%20see%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&behaviorActual=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20is%20currently%20wrong%20or%20missing%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&reproducer=%3C!--%20list%20steps%20in%20the%20application%20that%20show%20behavior%20that%20should%20be%20documented%20--%3E" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Report an issue</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Each realm created on the Keycloak has a dedicated Admin Console from which that realm can be managed.
The <code>master</code> realm is a special realm that allows admins to manage more than one realm on the system.
You can also
define fine-grained access to users in different realms to manage the server.
This chapter goes over all the scenarios for this.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect2">
<h3 id="_master_realm_access_control"><a class="anchor" href="#_master_realm_access_control"></a>Master realm access control</h3>
<div class="sidebarblock page-links">
<div class="content">
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/tree/main/docs/documentation/server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions/master-realm.adoc" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Edit this section</a>
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/new?template=bug.yml&title=Docs:%20server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions/master-realm.adoc&description=%0A%0AFile:%20server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions/master-realm.adoc&version=26.8.1&behaviorExpected=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20you%20want%20to%20see%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&behaviorActual=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20is%20currently%20wrong%20or%20missing%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&reproducer=%3C!--%20list%20steps%20in%20the%20application%20that%20show%20behavior%20that%20should%20be%20documented%20--%3E" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Report an issue</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <code>master</code> realm in Keycloak is a special realm and treated differently than other realms.
Users in the Keycloak <code>master</code> realm can be granted permission to manage zero or more realms that are deployed on the Keycloak server.
When a realm is created, Keycloak automatically creates various roles that grant permissions to access that new realm.
Access to The Admin Console and Admin REST endpoints can be controlled by mapping these roles to users in the <code>master</code> realm.
It’s possible to create multiple superusers,  as well as users that can only manage specific realms.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="global-roles"><a class="anchor" href="#global-roles"></a>Global roles</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>There are two realm-level roles in the <code>master</code> realm.
These are:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>admin</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>create-realm</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Users with the <code>admin</code> role are superusers and have full access to manage any realm on the server.  Users with the <code>create-realm</code> role
are allowed to create new realms.  They will be granted full access to any new realm they create.</p>
</div>
<div class="admonitionblock important">
<table>
<tr>
<td class="icon">
<i class="fa icon-important" title="Important"></i>
</td>
<td class="content">
Admins with the <code>create-realm</code> role who do not have the <code>admin</code> role will also need the realm-specific <code>query-realms</code> role to be able to create and list realms in the Admin Console.
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="realm-specific-roles"><a class="anchor" href="#realm-specific-roles"></a>Realm specific roles</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Admin users within the <code>master</code> realm can be granted management privileges to one or more other realms in the system.
Each realm in Keycloak is represented by a client in the <code>master</code> realm.
The name of the client is <code><realm name>-realm</code>.  These clients each have client-level roles defined which define varying
level of access to manage an individual realm.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The roles available are:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>create-client</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>impersonation</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-authorization</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-clients</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-events</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-identity-providers</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-organizations</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-realm</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-users</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-clients</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-groups</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-organizations</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-realms</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-users</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-authorization</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-clients</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-events</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-identity-providers</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-organizations</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-realm</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-users</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Assign the roles you want to your users and they will only be able to use that specific part of the administration console.</p>
</div>
<div class="admonitionblock important">
<table>
<tr>
<td class="icon">
<i class="fa icon-important" title="Important"></i>
</td>
<td class="content">
Admins with the <code>manage-users</code> role will only be able to assign admin roles to users that they themselves have.  So, if an admin has the <code>manage-users</code> role but doesn’t have the <code>manage-realm</code> role, they will not be able to assign this role.
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="granting-admin-roles-to-users"><a class="anchor" href="#granting-admin-roles-to-users"></a>Granting admin roles to users</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When granting admin roles to users in a realm, you must explicitly assign these roles to the user, either by a direct
role mapping (including roles granted via identity provider mappers) or by assigning the user to a group that has the appropriate role mappings.
This is true even for users in the <code>master</code> realm.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Even though you are able to create client protocol mappers for a client to map admin roles to tokens, the admin roles
will be ignored when the user authenticates and will not be included in the token.  This is because admin roles are only
used for authorization to access the Admin Console and Admin REST endpoints, and are not intended to be used for
application access control.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Effectively, access to the Admin API is only granted to users with admin roles explicitly assigned through direct role
mappings or group memberships, and not to users with admin roles mapped only through client protocol mappers.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="multi-realm-administration-considerations"><a class="anchor" href="#multi-realm-administration-considerations"></a>Multi-realm administration considerations</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <code>admin</code> role in the <code>master</code> realm is a composite role. For every realm in the deployment, it includes
the full set of admin roles from that realm’s <code><realm name>-realm</code> client. For example, with 100 realms,
the <code>admin</code> composite contains over 2,000 role mappings (approximately 21 roles per realm). This has
implications for token size and performance.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="token-size"><a class="anchor" href="#token-size"></a>Token size</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When using full (non-lightweight) access tokens, all admin roles from the <code>admin</code> composite are included
in the token. With hundreds of realms, the token can exceed HTTP header size limits enforced by load
balancers or reverse proxies.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>To mitigate this, use lightweight access tokens. The <code>security-admin-console</code> and <code>admin-cli</code> clients use
lightweight access tokens by default since Keycloak 26. Lightweight tokens do not carry roles over
the wire — the server resolves them from the user session when needed.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="cache-sizing"><a class="anchor" href="#cache-sizing"></a>Cache sizing</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Deployments with many realms should ensure that the <code>realms</code>, <code>users</code>, and <code>authorization</code> local caches are
properly sized. Undersized caches lead to frequent evictions and cache misses, resulting in additional
database round-trips that degrade performance. See the <a href="https://www.keycloak.org/server/caching">server caching guide</a>
for guidance on tuning cache sizes.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="role-policies-and-fine-grained-admin-permissions"><a class="anchor" href="#role-policies-and-fine-grained-admin-permissions"></a>Role policies and fine-grained admin permissions</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When using <a href="https://www.keycloak.org/docs/26.8.1/server_admin/#_fine_grained_permissions">fine-grained admin permissions</a>, the effective admin roles considered
by role policies are the intersection of the roles present in the token and the roles the user actually has. Because
the token reflects the authenticating client’s scope and protocol mapper configuration, the same user can have
different effective roles depending on which client they authenticate with.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>Fetch Roles</strong> setting on role policies controls whether this intersection is applied. When <strong>Fetch Roles</strong> is
disabled (the default), only roles that are both assigned to the user and present in the token are considered.
When <strong>Fetch Roles</strong> is enabled, roles are resolved directly from the user’s role assignments, bypassing the token
and any client scope filtering.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>For deployments where multiple clients authenticate administrators with different levels of access, keep
<strong>Fetch Roles</strong> disabled on role policies so that client scope constrains which admin roles are considered
for authorization decisions. This ensures that a client with a restricted scope cannot be used to exercise
permissions beyond what its scope allows, even if the authenticating user holds broader role assignments.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect2">
<h3 id="_per_realm_admin_permissions"><a class="anchor" href="#_per_realm_admin_permissions"></a>Dedicated realm admin consoles</h3>
<div class="sidebarblock page-links">
<div class="content">
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/tree/main/docs/documentation/server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions/per-realm.adoc" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Edit this section</a>
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/new?template=bug.yml&title=Docs:%20server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions/per-realm.adoc&description=%0A%0AFile:%20server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions/per-realm.adoc&version=26.8.1&behaviorExpected=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20you%20want%20to%20see%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&behaviorActual=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20is%20currently%20wrong%20or%20missing%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&reproducer=%3C!--%20list%20steps%20in%20the%20application%20that%20show%20behavior%20that%20should%20be%20documented%20--%3E" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Report an issue</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Each realm has a dedicated Admin Console that can be accessed by going to the url <code>/admin/{realm-name}/console</code>.
Users within that realm can be granted realm management permissions by assigning specific user role mappings.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Each realm has a built-in client called <code>realm-management</code>.  You can view this client by going to the
<code>Clients</code> left menu item of your realm.  This client defines client-level roles that specify permissions that can be granted to manage the realm.</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>create-client</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>impersonation</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-authorization</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-clients</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-events</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-identity-providers</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-organizations</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-realm</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>manage-users</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-clients</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-groups</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-organizations</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-realms</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>query-users</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>realm-admin</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-authorization</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-clients</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-events</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-identity-providers</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-organizations</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-realm</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>view-users</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Assign the roles you want to your users and they will only be able to use that specific part of the administration console.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect2">
<h3 id="_fine_grained_permissions"><a class="anchor" href="#_fine_grained_permissions"></a>Delegating realm administration using permissions</h3>
<div class="sidebarblock page-links">
<div class="content">
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/tree/main/docs/documentation/server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions/fine-grain-v2.adoc" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Edit this section</a>
<a href="https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/new?template=bug.yml&title=Docs:%20server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions/fine-grain-v2.adoc&description=%0A%0AFile:%20server_admin/topics/admin-console-permissions/fine-grain-v2.adoc&version=26.8.1&behaviorExpected=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20you%20want%20to%20see%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&behaviorActual=%3C!--%20describe%20what%20is%20currently%20wrong%20or%20missing%20in%20the%20docs%20--%3E&reproducer=%3C!--%20list%20steps%20in%20the%20application%20that%20show%20behavior%20that%20should%20be%20documented%20--%3E" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Report an issue</a>
</div>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>You can delegate realm management to other administrators, the realm administrators, using the fine-grained admin permissions
feature.
Different from the Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) Mechanism provided through the
<a href="#_master_realm_access_control">Global and Realm specific roles</a>, this feature provides a more fine-grained control over
how realm resources can be accessed and managed based on a well-defined set of operations that can be performed on them.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>By relying on a Policy-Based Access Control, realm administrators can define permissions to realm resources such as users,
groups, and clients, using different policy types, or access control methods, so that a realm administrator is limited to
access a subset of realm resources and their operations.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The feature provides an alternative to the aforementioned RBAC mechanism, but it does
not replace it. You are still able to grant administrative roles like <code>view-users</code> or <code>manage-clients</code> to delegate access
to realm administrators but doing so will skip the mechanisms provided by this feature.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Enforcing access to realm resources only applies when managing resources through the administration console or the Admin API.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="_understanding_different_types_realm_admins_"><a class="anchor" href="#_understanding_different_types_realm_admins_"></a>Understanding the different types of realm administrators</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>There are three different types of realm administrators when managing a realm:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Server administrators</strong>: These are users (or service accounts) that have been granted with the <code>admin</code> role in the master realm.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Realm administrators</strong>: These are users (or service accounts) that have been granted with the <code>realm-admin</code> role in a specific realm.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Delegated realm administrators</strong>: These are users (or service accounts) other than the types above but granted access to manage
a realm through the fine-grained admin permissions feature.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Both server and realm administrators can manage a realm with full access to all their resources and
administrative operations. The main difference between them is that server administrators can manage any realm in the server, while realm administrators can only manage
the realm they have been granted access to.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Delegated realm administrators, on the other hand, can have limited access to a realm based on the permissions defined through this feature.
They can only access the resources and operations they have been granted access to.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Be aware that both server and realm administrators are not affected by the permissions you define when managing access to realm resources through this feature.
Always make sure to review the users granted with the <code>admin</code> or <code>realm-admin</code> roles to avoid any potential privilege escalation.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="_understanding_realm_resource_types"><a class="anchor" href="#_understanding_realm_resource_types"></a>Understanding the Realm Resource Types</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>In a realm, you can manage different types of resources such as users, groups, clients, client scopes, roles, and so on.
As a realm administrator, you are constantly managing these resources when managing identities and how they authenticate
and are authorized to access a realm and applications.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>This feature provides the necessary mechanisms to enforce access controls when managing realm resources, limited to:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>Users</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Groups</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Clients</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Roles</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Organizations</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>You can manage permissions for all resources of a given resource type, such as all users in a realm, or
for a specific realm resource, such as a specific user or set of users in the realm.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="understanding-the-scopes-of-access"><a class="anchor" href="#understanding-the-scopes-of-access"></a>Understanding the scopes of access</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Each realm resource supports a well-defined set of management operations, or scopes, that can be performed on them,
such as <code>view</code>, <code>manage</code>, and resource-specific operations such as <code>view-members</code>, if you take groups as an example.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When managing permissions, you are selecting a set of one or more scopes from a resource type to allow realm administrators
to perform specific operations on a resource type. For instance, granting a <code>view</code> scope will give access to realm administrators
to list, search, and view a realm resource. On the other hand, the <code>manage</code> scope will allow administrators to perform updates
and deletes on them.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The scopes are completely independent of each other. If you give access to <code>manage</code> a realm resource, that does not mean the
<code>view</code> scope is granted automatically. No transitive dependency exists between scopes. Although this might impact the
overall user experience when managing permissions because you need to select individual scopes,
the benefit is that you can more easily identify the permissions that enforce access to a specific scope.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Certain scopes from a resource type have a relationship (not a transitive dependency) to scopes in another resource type.
This relationship is mainly true when you manage a resource type that represents a group of realm resources, such as realm groups
and their members.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="users-resource-type"><a class="anchor" href="#users-resource-type"></a>Users Resource Type</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>Users</strong> realm resource type represents the users in a realm. You can manage permissions for users based on the following
set of scopes:</p>
</div>
<table class="tableblock frame-all grid-all stretch">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 30%;">
<col style="width: 50%;">
<col style="width: 20%;">
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Scope</strong></th>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Description</strong></th>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Also granted by</strong></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>view</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can view users. This scope should be set whenever you want to make users available from queries.</p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><code>view-members</code></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>manage</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can manage and create users.</p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><code>manage-members</code></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>manage-group-membership</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can assign or unassign users to/from groups.</p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><code>manage-membership-of-members</code></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>map-roles</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can assign or unassign roles to/from users.</p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">None</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>impersonate</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can impersonate other users.</p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><code>impersonate-members</code></p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>reset-password</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can reset user passwords. If no permission with <code>reset-password</code> is found, it falls back to check <code>manage</code> scope.</p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">None</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The user resource type has a strong relationship with some of the permissions you can set to groups. Most of the time,
users are members of groups and granting access to <code>view-members</code> or <code>manage-members</code> of a group should also allow
a realm administrator to <code>view</code> and <code>manage</code> members of that group. Note that <code>manage</code> for users includes creating new users.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>To assign or unassign a specific user to or from a group, both sides of the relationship are required: <code>manage-group-membership</code>
on the user and <code>manage-membership</code> on the target group.
The <code>manage-membership-of-members</code> scope can be used to grant or deny <code>manage-group-membership</code> based on the groups that
the target user currently belongs to.</p>
</div>
<div class="admonitionblock note">
<table>
<tr>
<td class="icon">
<i class="fa icon-note" title="Note"></i>
</td>
<td class="content">
<div class="paragraph">
<p>This feature does not support enforcing access to federated resources.
Users from external storage providers (such as LDAP with import disabled) are not visible
in search results when access is controlled through fine-grained permissions.
To include federated users in search results, grant the administrator the <code>view-users</code> role,
or enable user import on the federation provider.</p>
</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="groups-resource-type"><a class="anchor" href="#groups-resource-type"></a>Groups Resource Type</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>Groups</strong> realm resource type represents the groups in a realm. You can manage permissions for groups based on the following
set of management operations:</p>
</div>
<table class="tableblock frame-all grid-all stretch">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 30%;">
<col style="width: 70%;">
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Operation</strong></th>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Description</strong></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>view</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can view groups. This scope should be set whenever you want
                              to make groups available from queries.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>manage</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can manage groups.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>view-members</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can view group members.
                              This operation applies to any child group in the group hierarchy.
                              This can be prevented by explicitly denying permission for specific subgroups.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>manage-members</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can manage group members. Together with <code>manage-membership</code> and <code>view</code> on the group, also allows creating new users as members of the group.
                              This operation applies to any child group in the group hierarchy.
                              This can be prevented by explicitly denying permission for specific subgroups.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>impersonate-members</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can impersonate group members.
                              This operation applies to any child group in the group hierarchy.
                              This can be prevented by explicitly denying permission for specific subgroups.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>manage-membership</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can add or remove members from groups.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>manage-membership-of-members</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can grant or deny <code>manage-group-membership</code> for members of a group.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="admonitionblock note">
<table>
<tr>
<td class="icon">
<i class="fa icon-note" title="Note"></i>
</td>
<td class="content">
<div class="paragraph">
<p>To create a new user directly as a member of a group, the delegated administrator needs <code>manage-members</code>, <code>manage-membership</code>, and <code>view</code> scopes on the target group. The <code>view</code> scope is required because the group must be resolvable from queries during user creation.</p>
</div>
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>
<div class="sect5">
<h6 id="group-hierarchy-and-permission-inheritance"><a class="anchor" href="#group-hierarchy-and-permission-inheritance"></a>Group hierarchy and permission inheritance</h6>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <code>view-members</code>, <code>manage-members</code>, and <code>impersonate-members</code> scopes cascade through the group hierarchy. When you grant or deny one of these scopes on a group, the permission applies to all descendant groups unless a more specific permission exists on a descendant.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><strong>Deny cascading:</strong> A deny on a parent group prevents access to members of the parent and all its descendant groups (children, grandchildren, and so on).</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><strong>Allow carve-outs:</strong> You can override a parent deny by granting an explicit allow for the same scope on a specific child group. The allow applies only to direct members of that child group. It does not cascade further to the child’s own descendants. Members of deeper descendant groups remain denied unless they also have an explicit allow.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>A direct <code>view</code> permission on a specific user does not override a group membership deny that uses a member scope. Denies on the member scopes (<code>view-members</code>, <code>manage-members</code>, and <code>impersonate-members</code>)
take precedence over user-level permissions. The only way to restore access to a user in a denied group subtree is to grant an explicit allow for a member scope (such as <code>view-members</code>)
on the specific group the user belongs to.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Only the member scopes protect a group’s members. A group permission that denies only a <code>view</code> or <code>manage</code> scope,
does not block a user-level operation on a member of that group. In that case the user remains accessible through the
corresponding user-level permission, and the group the administrator cannot access is simply filtered out from the user’s
group memberships.
For example, an administrator with <code>view</code> on all users can still view a user who also belongs to a group they cannot access.
Only the groups the administrator is allowed to see are returned for that user.
Denying <code>view-members</code> (or <code>manage-members</code>) on that group is what protects its members and denies access to the user.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>For example, given a hierarchy <code>Department > Team A > Subteam X</code>:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>Denying <code>view-members</code> on <code>Department</code> denies access to members of <code>Department</code>, <code>Team A</code>, and <code>Subteam X</code>.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Adding an explicit allow for <code>view-members</code> on <code>Team A</code> restores access to direct members of <code>Team A</code> only. Members of <code>Subteam X</code> remain denied.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>To also restore access to <code>Subteam X</code> members, you must add a separate allow for <code>view-members</code> on <code>Subteam X</code>.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Granting a direct <code>view</code> permission on a specific user in <code>Team A</code> does not restore access if the group deny is in effect.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect5">
<h6 id="search-visibility-for-group-member-permissions"><a class="anchor" href="#search-visibility-for-group-member-permissions"></a>Search visibility for group member permissions</h6>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When <code>view-members</code> is granted on a parent group, members of child groups are accessible via direct user lookup (for example, <code>GET /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{userId}</code>) but may not appear in user search or count results. The search mechanism uses a partial evaluation that matches users against the specific groups referenced in the permission, not against their descendants.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>To ensure that members of child groups appear in search and count results, grant <code>view-members</code> on each child group explicitly.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When a delegated administrator has <code>view</code> permission on a group but not on its ancestor groups, the Admin REST API returns the full group hierarchy so the administrator can understand where the group belongs. Ancestor groups without <code>view</code> permission are returned as stripped representations containing only <code>id</code>, <code>name</code>, <code>path</code>, <code>parentId</code>, and <code>description</code>. Sensitive fields such as <code>attributes</code>, <code>realmRoles</code>, <code>clientRoles</code>, and <code>access</code> are omitted from these ancestors.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <code>subGroupCount</code> field on stripped ancestors reflects the number of visible children included in the response rather than the total child count. In the admin console, non-viewable ancestor groups appear greyed out and are not clickable.</p>
</div>
<div class="admonitionblock note">
<table>
<tr>
<td class="icon">
<i class="fa icon-note" title="Note"></i>
</td>
<td class="content">
When a delegated administrator has <code>view</code> permission only on groups that are not at the top level of the hierarchy, the admin console Groups page initially appears empty because only top-level groups are loaded on the initial page load. The administrator must use the search field to find their permitted groups. The search results then display the full hierarchy with stripped ancestors as described above.
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="clients-resource-type"><a class="anchor" href="#clients-resource-type"></a>Clients Resource Type</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>Clients</strong> realm resource type represents the clients in a realm. You can manage permissions for clients based on the following
set of management operations:</p>
</div>
<table class="tableblock frame-all grid-all stretch">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 30%;">
<col style="width: 70%;">
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Operation</strong></th>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Description</strong></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>view</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can view clients. This scope should be set whenever you want
                              to make clients available from queries.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>manage</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can manage clients.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>map-roles</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can assign any role defined by a client to a user.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>map-roles-composite</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can assign any role defined by a client as a composite to
                              another role.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>map-roles-client-scope</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Define if a realm administrator can assign any role defined by a client to a client scope.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>map-roles</strong> operation does not grant the ability to manage users or assign roles arbitrarily. The administrator must also
have user role mapping permissions on the user.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="roles-resource-type"><a class="anchor" href="#roles-resource-type"></a>Roles Resource Type</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>Roles</strong> realm resource type represents the roles in a realm. You can manage permissions for roles based on the following set of management operations:</p>
</div>
<table class="tableblock frame-all grid-all stretch">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 30%;">
<col style="width: 70%;">
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Operation</strong></th>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Description</strong></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>map-role</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can assign a role (or multiple roles) to a user.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>map-role-composite</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can assign a role (or multiple roles) as a composite to another role.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>map-role-client-scope</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can apply a role (or multiple roles) to a client scope.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>map-roles</strong> operation does not grant the ability to manage users or assign roles arbitrarily. The administrator must also
have user role mapping permissions on the user.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>An administrator granted the <strong>map-role</strong> operation on a role can also view that role, including its attributes and composites,
so that it can be selected when assigning roles to users and groups. There is no separate <strong>view</strong> operation for roles.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>If there is a client resource type permission for the <strong>map-roles</strong>, <strong>map-roles-composite</strong>, or <strong>map-roles-client-scope</strong> scopes,
it will take precedence over any role resource type permission if the role is a client role.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="organizations-resource-type"><a class="anchor" href="#organizations-resource-type"></a>Organizations Resource Type</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>Organizations</strong> realm resource type represents the organizations in a realm. You can manage permissions for organizations based on the following
set of management operations:</p>
</div>
<table class="tableblock frame-all grid-all stretch">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 30%;">
<col style="width: 70%;">
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Operation</strong></th>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Description</strong></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>view</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can view organizations. This scope should be set whenever you want
                              to make organizations available from queries.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>manage</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">Defines if a realm administrator can manage organizations, including updating and deleting them.</p></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Creating new organizations requires <code>manage</code> permission on all organizations (the resource type level), not just on a specific organization.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="enabling-admin-permissions-to-a-realm"><a class="anchor" href="#enabling-admin-permissions-to-a-realm"></a>Enabling admin permissions to a realm</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>To enable fine-grained admin permissions in a realm, follow these steps:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>Log in to the Admin Console.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Click <strong>Realm settings</strong>.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Enable <strong>Admin Permissions</strong> and click <strong>Save</strong>.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><span class="image"><img src="./images/fine-grain-enable.png" alt="Fine grain enable"></span></p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Once enabled, a <strong>Permissions</strong> section appears in the left-side menu of the administration console.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><span class="image"><img src="./images/fine-grain-permissions-tab.png" alt="Fine grain permissions tab"></span></p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>From this section, you can manage the permissions for realm resources.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="_managing-permissions"><a class="anchor" href="#_managing-permissions"></a>Managing Permissions</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>Permissions</strong> tab provides an overview of all active permissions within a realm. From here, administrators can create,
update, delete, or search for permissions. You can also pre-evaluate the permissions you have created to check
if they are enforcing access to realm resources as expected.
For more details, see <a href="#_evaluating-permissions">Evaluating Permissions</a>.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>To create a permission, click on the <code>Create permission</code> button and select the resource type you want to protect.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><span class="image"><img src="./images/select-resource-type.png" alt="Selecting a resource type to protect"></span></p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Once you select the resource type, you can now define how access should be enforced for a set of one or more resources of the selected type:</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><span class="image"><img src="./images/create-permission.png" alt="Creating a permission"></span></p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When managing a permission you can define the following settings:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Name</strong>: A unique name for the permission. The name should also not conflict with any policy name</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Description</strong>: An optional description to better describe what the permission is about</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Authorization scopes</strong>: A set of one or more scopes representing the operations you want to protect for the selected resource type.
An administrator must have explicit permission assigned for each operation to perform the corresponding action. For example,
assigning only <strong>manage</strong> without <strong>view</strong> will prevent the user from being visible.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Enforce access to</strong>: Defines if the permission should enforce access to all resources of the selected type or to specific resources in a realm.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Policies</strong>: Defines a set of one or more policies that should be evaluated to grant or deny access to the selected resource(s).</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>After creating the permission, it will automatically take effect when enforcing access to (all) resources and scopes you selected.
Keep that fact in mind when creating and updating permissions in production.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="defining-permissions-for-viewing-realm-resources"><a class="anchor" href="#defining-permissions-for-viewing-realm-resources"></a>Defining permissions for viewing realm resources</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>This feature relies on a partial evaluation mechanism to partially evaluate the permissions that a realm administrator has
when listing and viewing realm resources. This mechanism will pre-fetch all the permissions set for view-related scopes where the realm administrator
is referenced either directly or indirectly.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Permissions that grant access to <code>view</code> a realm resource of a certain type must use one of the following policies to
make them available from queries:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p><code>User</code></p>
</li>
<li>
<p><code>Group</code></p>
</li>
<li>
<p><code>Role</code></p>
</li>
<li>
<p><code>Aggregated</code></p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When using an <code>Aggregated</code> policy, underlying policies that support partial evaluation (<code>User</code>, <code>Group</code>, <code>Role</code>, or nested <code>Aggregated</code>)
are evaluated during partial evaluation. Underlying policies of other types (such as <code>Time</code> or <code>JavaScript</code>) are skipped
because they cannot be pre-evaluated at the database level. If an aggregated policy contains only unsupported policy types,
the entire aggregated policy is excluded from partial evaluation.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When an aggregated policy contains a mix of supported and unsupported policy types, only the supported policies contribute to the
decision. Unsupported policies do not count as grants but are still considered in the total policy count, which means <code>Unanimous</code>
and <code>Consensus</code> decision strategies become more conservative. For best results, use only <code>User</code>, <code>Group</code>, <code>Role</code>, or nested
<code>Aggregated</code> policies as the underlying policies of an aggregated policy used in view-related permissions.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>By using any of the policies above, Keycloak can pre-calculate the set of resources that a realm administration can view
by looking for a direct (if using a user policy) or indirect (if using a role or group policy) reference to the realm administrator.
Therefore, the partial evaluation mechanism involves decorating queries with access controls that will run at the database level. This capability is mainly important to
properly allow paginating resources as well as avoid an additional overhead on the server-side when evaluating permissions for each
realm resource returned by queries.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Partial evaluation and filtering occurs only if the feature is enabled to a realm, and if the user is not granted
with view-related administrative roles like <code>view-users</code> or <code>view-clients</code>. For instance, it will not happen for administrators granted
with the <code>admin</code> role at the master realm (server administrators), or realm administrators granted with the <code>realm-admin</code> role in a realm other than the master realm.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When querying resources, the partial evaluation mechanism works as follows:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>Resolve all the permissions for a certain resource type that reference the realm administrator</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Pre-evaluate each permission to check if the realm administrator does or does not have access to the resources associated with the permission</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Decorate database queries based on the resources granted or denied</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>As a result, the result set of a query will hold only the realm resources where realm administrators have access to any of the view-related scopes.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="searching-permissions"><a class="anchor" href="#searching-permissions"></a>Searching Permissions</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The Admin Console provides several ways to search for permissions, supporting the following capabilities:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>Search for permissions that contain a specific string in their <strong>Name</strong></p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Search for permissions of a specific resource type, such as <strong>Users</strong></p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Search for permissions of a specific resource type that apply to a particular resource (such as <strong>Users</strong> resource type for user <code>myadmin</code>).</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Search for permissions of a specific resource type with a given scope (such as <strong>Users</strong> resource type permissions with the <strong>manage</strong> scope).</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Search for permissions of a specific resource type that apply to a particular resource and have a specific scope (such as <strong>Users</strong> resource
type permissions with the <strong>manage</strong> scope for user <code>myadmin</code>).</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<div class="title">Fine grained permissions search</div>
<p><span class="image"><img src="./images/fine-grain-search.png" alt="Fine grained permissions search"></span></p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>These capabilities allow realm administrators to perform queries on their universe of permissions and identify which ones
are enforcing access to a set of one or more realm resources and their scopes. Combined with the evaluation tool on the
<strong>Evaluation</strong> tab, they provide a key management tool for managing permissions in a realm. See <a href="#_evaluating-permissions">Evaluating Permissions</a>
for more details.</p>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="managing-policies"><a class="anchor" href="#managing-policies"></a>Managing Policies</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>Policies</strong> tab allows administrators to define conditions using different access control methods to determine whether
a permission should be granted to an administrator attempting to perform operations on a realm resource. When managing permissions,
you must associate at least a single policy to grant or deny access to a realm resource.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Policies are basically conditions that will evaluate to either a <code>GRANT</code> or a <code>DENY</code>. Their outcome will decide whether
a permission should be granted or denied.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>A permission is only granted if all its associated policies evaluate to a <code>GRANT</code>. Otherwise, the permission is denied
and a realm administrator will not be able to access the protected resource.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Keycloak provides a set of built-in policies that you can choose from:</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p><span class="image"><img src="./images/select-policy-type.png" alt="Selecting a policy type"></span></p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Once you have a well-defined and stable permission model for your realm, less need exists to create policies. You can instead reuse existing policies to create more permissions.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>For more details about each policy type, see <a href="https://www.keycloak.org/docs/26.8.1/authorization_services/#_policy_overview">Managing policies</a>.</p>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="_evaluating-permissions"><a class="anchor" href="#_evaluating-permissions"></a>Evaluating Permissions</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The <strong>Evaluation</strong> tab provides a testing environment where administrators can verify that permissions are enforcing access
as expected. The administrator can see what permissions are involved when enforcing access to a particular resource and what the outcome is.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>You need to provide a set of fields in order to run an evaluation:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p><code>User</code>, the realm administrator or the subject trying to access a resource</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><code>Resource Type</code>, the resource type you want to evaluate</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><code>Resource Selector</code>, depending on the selected <code>Resource Type</code> you will be prompted to select a specific realm resource like a user, group, or client.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><code>Authorization scope</code>, the scope or the operation you want to evaluate. If not provided, the evaluation will happen for all the scopes of the selected resource type.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<div class="title">Fine grained permissions evaluation tab</div>
<p><span class="image"><img src="./images/fine-grain-evaluation.png" alt="Fine grained permissions evaluation tab"></span></p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>By clicking the <code>Evaluate</code> button, the server will evaluate all the permissions associated with the selected resource and scopes
just like if the selected <code>User</code> were trying to access the resource when using the administration console or the Admin API.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>For instance, in the example above you can see that the user <code>myadmin</code> can <strong>manage</strong> user <code>user-1</code> because a <code>Allow managing all realm users</code> permission
voted to a <code>PERMIT</code>, therefore granting access to the <code>manage</code> scope. However, all the other scopes were denied.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Combined with the searching capabilities from the <strong>Permissions</strong> tab, you can perform troubleshooting to identify any permission that
is not behaving as expected.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>When evaluating permissions, the following rules apply:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p>The outcome from resource-specific permissions have precedence over broader permissions that give access to all resources of a certain type</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>If no permissions exist for a specific resource, access will be granted based on the permission that grants access to all resources of a certain type</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>The outcome from different permissions that enforce access to a specific resource will only grant access if they all permit access to the resource</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="_resolving-conflicting-permissions"><a class="anchor" href="#_resolving-conflicting-permissions"></a>Resolving conflicting permissions</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Permissions can have multiple policies associated with them. As the authorization model evolves, it is common for some policies within a permission or
even different permissions related to a specific resource to conflict.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>The evaluation outcome will be "denied" whenever any permission is evaluated to "DENY." If there are multiple permissions related to the same resource,
all of them must grant access in order for the outcome to be "granted."</p>
</div>
<div class="admonitionblock important">
<table>
<tr>
<td class="icon">
<i class="fa icon-important" title="Important"></i>
</td>
<td class="content">
Fine-grained admin permissions allow you to set up permissions for individual resources or for the resource type itself (such as all users,
all groups, and so on.). If a permission or permissions related to a specific resource exist, the "all-resource" permission is <strong>NOT</strong> taken into account
during evaluation. If no specific permission exists, the fallback is to the "all-resource" permission. This approach helps address scenarios like
allowing members of the <code>realm-admins</code> group to manage members of realm groups, but preventing them from managing members of the <code>realm-admins</code> group
themselves.
</td>
</tr>
</table>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<div class="sect3">
<h4 id="_realm_access_control"><a class="anchor" href="#_realm_access_control"></a>Accessing a Realm administration console as a Realm Administrator</h4>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Realm administrators can access a dedicated realm-specific administration console that allows them to manage resources within their assigned realm.
This console is separate from the main Keycloak Admin Console, which is typically used by realm administrators.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>For more details on dedicated realm administration consoles and available roles, refer to: <a href="#_per_realm_admin_permissions">Dedicated admin consoles</a>.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>To access the administration console, a realm administrator must have at least one of the following roles assigned, depending on the resources they
need to administer:</p>
</div>
<div class="ulist">
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>query-users</strong> – Required to query realm users.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>query-groups</strong> – Required to query realm groups.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>query-clients</strong> – Required to query realm clients.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>query-organizations</strong> – Required to query realm organizations.</p>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>By granting any of these roles to a realm user, they will be able to access the administration console, but only for the
areas that correspond to roles granted. For instance, if you assign the <code>query-users</code> role, the realm administrator
will only have access to the <code>Users</code> section in the administration console. If an administrator is responsible for
multiple resource types (such as both users and groups), they must have all the corresponding "query-*" roles assigned.</p>
</div>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>These roles enable basic access to query resources but do not grant permission to view or modify them. To grant or deny access
to realm resources you need to set up the permissions for any of the operations available from each resource type.
For more details, see <a href="#_managing-permissions">Managing Permissions</a>.</p>
</div>
<div class="sect4">
<h5 id="roles-and-permission-relationship"><a class="anchor" href="#roles-and-permission-relationship"></a>Roles and Permission relationship</h5>
<div class="paragraph">
<p>Fine grained permissions are used to grant additional permissions. You cannot override the default behavior of the built-in admin roles.
If a realm administrator is assigned one or more admin roles, it prevents the permissions from being evaluated. This means that
if a respective admin role is assigned to a realm administrator, permission evaluation will be bypassed, and access will be granted.</p>
</div>
<table class="tableblock frame-all grid-all stretch">
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 30%;">
<col style="width: 70%;">
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Admin Role</strong></th>
<th class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><strong>Description</strong></th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>query-users</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">A realm administrator can see the <strong>Users</strong> section in administration console and can search for users in the realm.
                             It does not grant the ability to <strong>view</strong> users.</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock"><strong>query-groups</strong></p></td>
<td class="tableblock halign-left valign-top"><p class="tableblock">A realm administrator can see the <strong>Groups</strong> section in administration console and can search for groups in the realm.
